cards.front: What are the three rungs of the ladder of evidence for where a memory lives, from lowest to highest?
cards.back: Correlation, sufficiency and necessity. The upper two are interventions that answer different questions, so neither alone locates a memory.
cards.quote: Correlation is the lowest rung. The upper two are both interventions that answer different questions, so neither alone locates a memory.
cards.section: Three puzzles and a ladder of evidence

cards.front: Silencing a set of cells while an animal remembers by itself impairs recall. What does this show, and what does it not show?
cards.back: It shows the animal uses those cells for recall at that moment (necessity). It does not show the memory was erased or stored in them.
cards.quote: This shows the animal uses them at that moment, not that the memory was erased.
cards.section: Three puzzles and a ladder of evidence

cards.front: In the guiding model of memory, how does a partial cue bring back a whole memory?
cards.back: Learning strengthens links among cells active together, leaving a linked group. In a recurrent network, a fragment close enough to the group's pattern pulls the rest back on: the group completes itself.
cards.quote: On this model, recall from a cue is the group completing itself.
cards.section: Three puzzles and a ladder of evidence

cards.front: Place cells are hippocampal neurons that fire when the animal is in one region of an environment, the cell's {{c1::place field}}.
cards.quote: These became place cells: hippocampal neurons that fire when the animal is in one region of an environment, the cell's place field.
cards.section: Place and grid cells: candidate members of a group

cards.front: Why is a place-cell rate map built by dividing each bin's spike count by the time the rat spent in that bin?
cards.back: Spikes pile up wherever the rat lingers, whether or not the cell prefers that spot. Dividing by time gives a rate (spikes per second) that reflects the cell, not the rat's dwelling.
cards.quote: Dots pile up wherever the rat lingered, whether or not the cell cares about that spot.
cards.section: Reading a rate map

cards.front: A rat place cell fires 12 spikes in bin A, where the rat spent 4 s, and 30 spikes in bin B, where it spent 15 s. Which bin is hotter on the rate map?
cards.back: Bin A. A: 12/4 = 3 spikes per second. B: 30/15 = 2 spikes per second. B has more spikes only because the rat stayed longer.
cards.quote: So divide the floor into bins, and for each bin divide the spikes by the seconds spent there.
cards.section: Reading a rate map

cards.front: A hippocampal cell fires only when a rat is in one corner of a box. What does this show, and what does it not show?
cards.back: A correlation between firing and position. It does not show the cell encodes only position, or that the animal uses it to navigate.
cards.quote: A cell that fires in one place is a correlation between firing and position.
cards.section: Reading a rate map

cards.front: What firing pattern defines a grid cell in the rat medial entorhinal cortex?
cards.back: It fires at many places in an enclosure, and those places form a lattice of roughly equilateral triangles.
cards.quote: These grid cells fired at many places, and the places formed a lattice of roughly equilateral triangles.
cards.section: Grid cells and the autocorrelogram

cards.front: The spatial autocorrelogram of a rat entorhinal cell's rate map shows a central peak and a ring of six peaks at multiples of 60 degrees, each about 50 cm from the centre. Interpret it.
cards.back: The cell is a grid cell: a triangular lattice of firing fields gives six peaks at 60-degree steps. The centre-to-ring distance is the grid spacing, here about 50 cm.
cards.why: The central peak is the zero shift, where the map matches itself.
cards.quote: Around it, a triangular lattice gives a ring of six peaks, at angles that are multiples of 60 degrees.
cards.section: Grid cells and the autocorrelogram

cards.front: A model says rat grid cells simply feed place cells. The hippocampus is silenced while grid cells are recorded. What happens to the grid pattern, and what does it mean for the model?
cards.back: The grid pattern is erased. So the hippocampus also shapes grid firing; the two systems shape each other rather than grid cells simply feeding place cells.
cards.why: In rat pups, place firing also appears before stable grid firing.
cards.quote: In rat pups, place firing appears before stable grid firing, and silencing the hippocampus erases the grid pattern
cards.section: Grid cells and the autocorrelogram

cards.front: What did Donald Hebb propose in 1949 about connections between cells?
cards.back: When one cell repeatedly takes part in firing another, the first becomes more effective at driving the second.
cards.quote: In 1949 Donald Hebb proposed that when one cell repeatedly takes part in firing another, the first becomes more effective at driving the second.
cards.section: Strengthening the links

cards.front: Consolidation is the transformation of a temporary, labile memory into a {{c1::more stable form}}.
cards.quote: Consolidation is the transformation of a temporary, labile memory into a more stable form.
cards.section: Strengthening the links

cards.front: Contrast synaptic consolidation with systems consolidation: what changes, and over what time?
cards.back: Synaptic: stabilizes synaptic plasticity within hours of learning (late, protein-synthesis-dependent LTP). Systems: gradual reorganization of the brain systems that support a memory, over days to years.
cards.quote: Synaptic consolidation includes the processes that stabilize synaptic plasticity within hours of learning
cards.section: Strengthening the links

cards.front: A protein-synthesis inhibitor is given right after learning. Predict the effect on the strengthened synapses and on the memory a day later.
cards.back: The strengthened links would likely not be stabilized, so the memory would tend not to last.
cards.why: Synaptic consolidation includes protein-synthesis-dependent processes that stabilize synaptic plasticity within hours of learning, including late LTP.
cards.quote: the late, protein-synthesis-dependent phase of LTP you met in synaptic plasticity
cards.section: Strengthening the links

cards.front: Because CA3 has dense recurrent connections, it is often modelled as an {{c1::attractor network}}, in which a stored pattern is a stable state that activity falls into.
cards.quote: it is often modelled as an attractor network, in which a stored pattern is a stable state that activity falls into
cards.section: A network that completes itself

cards.front: In the Hopfield storage rule with ±1 units, what link do two units get if they agree in the stored pattern, and if they disagree?
cards.back: Agree: a positive link. Disagree: a negative link. Links are symmetric (1 to 2 equals 2 to 1).
cards.quote: Two units that agree in the pattern get a positive link, and two that disagree get a negative one.
cards.section: A network that completes itself

cards.front: A four-unit Hopfield network stores x = (1, 1, −1, −1) with w_ij = x_i x_j / 4, w_ii = 0, zero thresholds. Start at s = (1, 1, −1, 1). Compute the field on unit 4. What does unit 4 become?
cards.back: Row 4 is (−1/4, −1/4, +1/4, 0). h_4 = (−1/4)(1) + (−1/4)(1) + (1/4)(−1) = −3/4. Negative, so unit 4 flips to −1, restoring the stored pattern.
cards.quote: Thresholds are zero, and a unit keeps its old value if its field is exactly zero.
cards.section: A network that completes itself

cards.front: The four-unit Hopfield network storing x = (1, 1, −1, −1) is in state (1, 1, 1, 1). Each violated link adds 1/4 to the energy and each satisfied link subtracts 1/4. What is the energy? Check with the overlap formula.
cards.back: Links 1-2 and 3-4 (positive, units agree) are satisfied; the four negative links join agreeing units, so are violated. E = 4(1/4) − 2(1/4) = +0.5. Overlap = 0, so E = −(0 − 4)/8 = +0.5.
cards.quote: In this network each violated link adds 1/4 to the energy and each satisfied link subtracts 1/4.
cards.section: A network that completes itself

cards.front: In the four-unit Hopfield network, why must the energy fall each time a unit flips?
cards.back: A unit flips only when its field opposes it, meaning at least two of its three links are violated. Flipping satisfies those, so violations drop by at least one and energy falls by at least 1/2.
cards.quote: Flipping it satisfies those and violates the rest, so the violations drop by at least one and the energy falls by at least 1/2.
cards.section: A network that completes itself

cards.front: A four-unit Hopfield network stores only x = (1, 1, −1, −1). It starts at (−1, −1, 1, −1), and units update in order 1 to 4. Where does it end, and why?
cards.back: At (−1, −1, 1, 1), the inverted pattern. The cue is more wrong than right (3 of 4 units), and in a one-pattern network such a cue reaches the inverse, which is also stable.
cards.why: Fields in order: −1/4, −1/4, +1/4, +3/4, so only unit 4 flips.
cards.quote: a cue more wrong than right reaches its inverse
cards.section: A network that completes itself

cards.front: A large Hopfield-type network storing few patterns recalls correctly from a cue a third wrong. Many more patterns are then stored. Predict what happens to the same cue, and why.
cards.back: It is more likely to fail. Interference shrinks the basins, can remove stored valleys and adds spurious ones, so poorer cues fail first.
cards.why: A cue must start inside its pattern's basin; being closest is not enough when many patterns share the cells.
cards.quote: Storing more patterns reshapes the landscape: interference shrinks the basins, can remove some stored valleys, and adds spurious ones that mix stored patterns.
cards.section: A network that completes itself

cards.front: A model of CA3 stores many overlapping groups using only excitatory links and one fixed threshold. A weak partial cue is given. Predict the outcome with a low threshold, and with a high one.
cards.back: In some such models: a low threshold can let activity spread from the cued group into others, and a high one can leave a weak cue unable to recruit its group. Feedback inhibition that grows with total activity can keep activity sparse. Completion still depends on the connections, stored patterns, threshold and cue.
cards.quote: a low threshold lets activity spread from the cued group into others, while a high one leaves a weak cue unable to recruit its group
cards.section: A network that completes itself

cards.front: Mice lacking NMDA receptors only in CA3 pyramidal cells are tested in a water maze with all room cues and with only a fraction of them (Nakazawa and colleagues, 2002). What was found, and what does it suggest?
cards.back: Normal learning and recall with all cues, impaired recall with partial cues. This is the deficit an attractor model predicts, consistent with completion in CA3.
cards.why: Completion was inferred, not recorded in CA3; recordings in CA1 showed weaker place-cell activity under partial cues.
cards.quote: The mice learned a water-maze platform and recalled it normally with all the room cues, but were impaired when only a fraction of the cues remained.
cards.section: A network that completes itself

cards.front: How do the standard model and multiple-trace or transformation accounts differ on the hippocampus's role in old memories?
cards.back: Standard: the hippocampus is needed for a time, then cortex supports the memory alone. Multiple-trace: detailed episodic memories keep needing the hippocampus; a schematic version rests in cortex.
cards.quote: Multiple-trace and transformation accounts hold that detailed episodic memories keep needing the hippocampus, while a more schematic version comes to rest in cortex.
cards.section: Making a memory last: replay and ripples, from correlation to perturbation

cards.front: After hippocampal damage, a patient recalls the gist of an event from years ago but cannot recall recent events. How would the standard model and multiple-trace theory each read the spared old memory?
cards.back: Standard model: the old memory survives because cortex now holds it. Multiple-trace: what survives is mostly gist; vivid detail, even of old memories, still needs the hippocampus.
cards.quote: The standard model says their old memories survive because the cortex now holds them.
cards.section: Making a memory last: replay and ripples, from correlation to perturbation

cards.front: Wilson and McNaughton recorded many rat hippocampal cells in sleep before a spatial task, during it, and in sleep after. What did they find, and what kind of evidence is it?
cards.back: Pairs that co-fired during the task co-fired more in sleep after than before; task-silent pairs did not. It is pairwise correlation, not a decoded route or a test of memory.
cards.quote: Pairs that co-fired during the task were more likely to co-fire in the sleep after it than in the sleep before.
cards.section: Correlation in pairs: co-firing again in sleep

cards.front: In a rat sleep study, task-active cell pairs co-fire more in post-task sleep than in pre-task sleep, but task-silent pairs rise by the same amount. What does the silent-pair result undermine?
cards.back: The claim that the rise reflects the task experience. Silent pairs are the control; if they rise equally, something general about the later sleep could explain it.
cards.quote: Pairs silent during the task showed no such increase.
cards.section: Correlation in pairs: co-firing again in sleep

cards.front: In rats on a track, when are place-cell sequences replayed in reverse, and when forward (Diba and Buzsáki, 2007)?
cards.back: Reverse during pauses at the end of runs; forward before runs. Both are compressed in time.
cards.quote: compressed in time: in reverse during pauses at the end of runs, and forward before runs
cards.section: Correlation in order: sequences played forward and back

cards.front: What is a sharp-wave ripple in the CA1 local field potential, and when does it mostly occur?
cards.back: A slower sharp wave carrying a burst of fast waves, roughly 150 to 250 per second, lasting tens of milliseconds. Mostly when the animal is still: pausing, eating or in slow-wave sleep.
cards.quote: the ripple, roughly 150 to 250 per second, lasting tens of milliseconds
cards.section: Correlation in order: sequences played forward and back

cards.front: A lab cuts ripples short in rats' post-training sleep and sees worse performance next day, but its only control is unstimulated rats. What alternative remains, and what control did Girardeau and colleagues (2009) use?
cards.back: The stimulation itself, including any damage, could cause the deficit. Control: the same number of stimuli delivered at a delay after ripples. Only ripple-cutting rats were impaired, so timing on the ripples matters.
cards.quote: Selective elimination of the ripples impaired performance, and the delayed controls were not impaired.
cards.section: Turning it off: cut the ripples short

cards.front: Fernández-Ruiz and colleagues (2019) used closed-loop optogenetic stimulation to prolong ripples in awake rats. What happened, and what did it not test?
cards.back: Maze working-memory performance improved. It tested awake ripples in a working-memory task, not consolidation during sleep.
cards.quote: That tested awake ripples in a working-memory task, not consolidation during sleep
cards.section: Turning it off: cut the ripples short

cards.front: Ripple-disruption experiments impair later memory. What do they leave unshown?
cards.back: They remove ripple-linked activity in general, not one sequence, and they measured behaviour, not cortical change. They show ripple-linked activity matters, not how the hippocampus might teach the cortex.
cards.quote: They show that ripple-linked activity matters, not how the hippocampus might teach the cortex.
cards.section: Turning it off: cut the ripples short

cards.front: Place the replay evidence on the ladder of evidence: which rung do the sleep co-firing and sequence studies reach, and which rung does ripple disruption test?
cards.back: Co-firing (Wilson and McNaughton) and decoded sequences (Diba and Buzsáki) are correlation. Cutting ripples short (Girardeau) turns ripple activity off, a test of necessity. Prolonging awake ripples tested working memory, not sleep consolidation.
cards.quote: The evidence for replay climbs from correlation to turning ripple activity off, a test of necessity.
cards.section: Making a memory last: replay and ripples, from correlation to perturbation

cards.front: Why can the simple symmetric Hopfield rule store a group but not replay its cells in order, as place-cell sequences are replayed?
cards.back: The rule uses agreement alone and symmetric links, so it carries no information about which cell fires first. Ordered replay needs more than this simple model, for example links that care which cell fires first, as Hebb's own proposal and spike-timing rules do.
cards.quote: Replaying cells in order needs more than the simple model above, such as links that care which cell fires first.
cards.section: Making a memory last: replay and ripples, from correlation to perturbation

cards.front: Suppose the hippocampus teaches the cortex by replay during sleep. Predict the effect of cutting ripples short in the nights after mouse contextual fear learning on the remote (day-12) prefrontal requirement, and say what rules this rests on.
cards.back: Prefrontal members might mature less, weakening remote recall. Rests on the replay-teaching proposal plus Kitamura's maturing prefrontal engram. Disruption studies measured behaviour, not cortex, so this is untested.
cards.quote: One proposal is that the hippocampus teaches the cortex by replaying experience after it happens.
cards.section: Making a memory last: replay and ripples, from correlation to perturbation

cards.front: How do Kitamura and colleagues define engram cells?
cards.back: Cells activated by learning that undergo lasting change and can be reactivated by part of the original stimulus.
cards.quote: cells activated by learning that undergo lasting change and can be reactivated by part of the original stimulus
cards.section: Engrams: enough does not prove needed

cards.front: How does the c-fos promoter plus doxycycline system tag the mouse neurons active during one experience?
cards.back: The promoter of c-fos, an immediate early gene turned on in recently active neurons, is used to put the opsin into active cells. Doxycycline blocks the tag; removing it opens a labelling window, and giving it back closes it.
cards.quote: Doxycycline blocks the tag. Take it away and a window opens in which active cells get labelled.
cards.section: Sufficiency: turn the tagged cells on

cards.front: Liu and colleagues (2012) tagged mouse dentate-gyrus cells active during fear conditioning with channelrhodopsin-2. What did light do, which two controls made it specific, and what does it show?
cards.back: Light evoked freezing in a different context. Cells tagged in a neutral context, and EYFP-only conditioned mice, did not cause freezing. Activating the cells is enough to drive the behaviour: sufficiency.
cards.quote: Two controls made it specific: cells tagged in a neutral context did not evoke fear freezing
cards.section: Sufficiency: turn the tagged cells on

cards.front: Design a test of whether mice need tagged fear-conditioning cells for natural recall. Name the manipulation, the cue and the key control.
cards.back: Tag the cells with an inhibitory opsin, return the mouse to the conditioning box (natural cue), and silence them with light. Control: fluorophore-only mice given the same light. Freezing drops only in opsin mice means necessity.
cards.quote: Tag the cells with an inhibitory opsin instead, a light-driven protein that silences the cell.
cards.section: Necessity: silence the cells during natural recall

cards.front: Silencing tagged cells lowers freezing to the conditioning box in opsin mice only. What additional checks are needed before calling it a recall deficit?
cards.back: Check that silencing does not reduce movement or freezing to another feared cue. Either would point to impaired fear expression rather than recall.
cards.quote: Check that silencing does not reduce movement or freezing to another feared cue, which would point to fear expression rather than recall.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Mouse prefrontal cells active at contextual fear learning are tagged with an inhibitory opsin. In made-up data, day 3: light-off 50% freezing, light-on 48%; day 14: light-off 60%, light-on 15%. Give the fractional reduction each day and interpret.
cards.back: Day 3: (50 − 48)/50 = 4%. Day 14: (60 − 15)/60 = 75%. The cells are needed for remote, not recent, recall, as Kitamura found and the standard model predicts.
cards.quote: silencing the tagged prefrontal cells left recall intact on day 2 and disrupted it on day 12
cards.section: Necessity: silence the cells during natural recall

cards.front: Kitamura's prefrontal cells needed for remote recall on day 12 had been tagged at learning. What does this say about how the cortical part of the memory forms?
cards.back: It formed at once and matured, rather than first appearing after a later transfer. Their dendritic-spine density was higher by day 12.
cards.quote: The cortical part of the memory did not first appear after a later transfer. It formed at once and matured.
cards.section: Necessity: silence the cells during natural recall

cards.front: Using the idea of a memory as a self-completing group of cells, explain why driving one region's engram cells can evoke recall while silencing them may not block it.
cards.back: If the group spans several regions, driving one part can complete the whole, while silencing one part may leave enough of the rest to complete it. Consistent with this, reactivating several ensembles gave more recall (Roy 2022).
cards.quote: If a memory's group spans several regions, driving one part can complete the whole.
cards.section: Necessity: silence the cells during natural recall

cards.front: In mouse contextual fear, by day 15 the natural cue reactivates tagged dentate cells less, yet light on them still drives freezing, and tagged prefrontal cells have become necessary. What does this say about where the memory is?
cards.back: The answer depends on when you ask. The group is not fixed in one place: prefrontal members recruited at learning become needed over time, while dentate cells stay sufficient though less used naturally.
cards.quote: So, in this mouse paradigm, "where is the memory?" has an answer that depends on when you ask.
cards.section: Necessity: silence the cells during natural recall

cards.front: Tagged mouse engram cells pass sufficiency and necessity tests. What more is needed to claim the memory is stored in them?
cards.back: A measured change in the tagged cells, such as higher spine density or stronger synapses onto them, and a demonstration that blocking that change blocks the memory.
cards.quote: and a demonstration that blocking that change blocks the memory
cards.section: Design problem
